cells.tense: You are holding what was handed to you, and the form is steady in your arms.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: Choose a custom or story your people keep, and stay with it through the next stretch when it feels hollow. Keep it going. Don't repair what's thin in it yet.
cells.core:
You can carry what your people hand down without gripping it so hard it cracks. The form stays; the warmth inside it stays. That's not hardness — it's a load that knows how to give at the edges. The ritual you keep still leaves space for whoever is standing nearby, and they can feel that, not just follow it.

Your strength here is built to be shared, not decided alone. So let someone reach you in it. Choose one of the sayings or observances you keep — a meal, a phrase, a way of marking a day — and stay in contact with it through a hard stretch instead of setting it down or forcing it back to life. Let it be touched by what you and the others are carrying now. What holds will show itself without your hand closing on it.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the form steady and still let it move.
cells.verb: bearing what is handed down, holding a form steady while it passes to the next
cells.place: the shared ground where meaning is kept and handed forward

cells.tense: Soon you will be gripping the old forms hard enough that nothing new can enter them.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Look at how your shared life is arranged — who does what, who carries which part — and adjust the share once so it's fair. Then stop tuning. Leave the rest alone.
cells.core:
You can feel yourself bracing ahead, holding the line on how things have been done. The grip is strong, and from the outside it looks like the custom itself stiffening, not you. What was resilience starts to look like rigidity, and the people who love the thing you're protecting start to drift from it.

That grip isn't wrong, it's just out of proportion. Something in how your shared life is arranged has gone lopsided, and the fix isn't tighter holding. Look at one arrangement — who does what, who carries which part — and adjust the share once so it's fair between the people involved. Just that. Then stop. Holding the old shape past the point where it fits serves the shape, not the people.
cells.sheetLine: What you grip to save, you're squeezing out of shape.
cells.verb: bearing what is handed down, holding a form steady while it passes to the next
cells.place: the shared ground where meaning is kept and handed forward

cells.tense: You set the load down a while back, and you have been standing in the draft since.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Stop doing one customary thing — a greeting, a small observance, a phrase — for a week, on purpose. Notice the space it leaves. Then decide whether it comes back.
cells.core:
You used to carry what your people handed down, and somewhere you handed it off. Not to anyone else — you just stopped holding it. The meals, the phrases that used to come without thinking. You're upright, but the load isn't across your shoulders, and behind it there's a door you haven't looked at in a while.

What's meant to come next isn't carrying it harder. Something has finished, and your hands know it. Stop doing one customary thing — a greeting, a small family observance — for a week, deliberately. Just that. Leave the space where it was, and see whether it asks to come back or whether the room is lighter without it. Either answer is a place to stand.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped carrying it and said nothing about it.
cells.verb: bearing what is handed down, holding a form steady while it passes to the next
cells.place: the shared ground where meaning is kept and handed forward

cells.tense: You keep the old forms going, and you have not once called it strength.
cells.act: remember what drew you and face it again
cells.ask: Think of a tradition someone first showed you. Sit with the memory of them doing it, and feel again the pull that first made you pick it up.
cells.core:
Ask about the words you remember, the date you keep, how the thing is done, and you'll say you just do it, or that it's not a big deal, or that somebody else really holds it. Keeping it going has kept happening, and has kept happening a long time. You're just the last person you credit for it.

There's a draw underneath this that you didn't call a draw. Something in it caught you early — a person, a way of doing it, a moment you wouldn't want to lose. Go back to that. Think of a tradition someone first showed you, sit with the memory of them doing it, and feel again the pull that first made you pick it up. Knowing what you're steering by is half of knowing you've been steering at all.
cells.sheetLine: You've been keeping it alive and calling it nothing.

attempts.check: The draft's riskiest claim is that the seat is 'culture' in the sense of shared traditions and rituals; the person may read 'culture' as something narrower (family, workplace, national) or broader than the reading's Bridge-stage sense of meaning carried between people. If the reading is wrong and the seat lands elsewhere, the asks still work: each is one small act done wherever meaning is shared by more than one person, and none requires the person to identify a tradition first. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any that presumes a group is already gathered; every ask here works even in a room of two, and the core should leave that open rather than assume a crowd.
